questions.question: Which statement is the Nash existence theorem for normal-form games $\langle N,\{S_i\},\{v_i\}\rangle$?
options: If $N$ and every $S_i$ are finite, the game has at least one Nash equilibrium in pure strategies.
If $N$ and every $S_i$ are finite, the game has at least one Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies.
If $N$ and every $S_i$ are finite, the game has exactly one Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies.
If every $S_i$ is an interval, the game has at least one Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies.

questions.question: A finite normal-form game is known to satisfy the Nash existence theorem. What does the theorem tell us about its Nash equilibria?
options: There is exactly one, and it is the profile that rational players will choose.
There is at least one in pure strategies, possibly with others in mixed strategies.
There is at least one in mixed strategies; nothing about how many or which is played.
Every equilibrium is in strictly mixed strategies, using all pure strategies.

questions.question: In Matching Pennies player 1 gets $1$ on a match and $-1$ otherwise, and player 2 gets the negative. What does this game show about the Nash existence theorem?
options: The theorem is false: this finite game has no Nash equilibrium.
The theorem requires symmetric payoffs, which zero-sum games lack.
The theorem applies only to games in which some player has a dominant strategy.
The guarantee needs mixed strategies: this finite game has no pure equilibrium.

questions.question: The Cournot duopoly, in which each firm chooses a quantity from $[0,\infty)$, has a Nash equilibrium. What does this show about the finiteness assumption of the Nash existence theorem?
options: Finiteness is necessary, so the Cournot equilibrium must be in mixed strategies.
Finiteness can be dropped from the theorem: every game has an equilibrium.
Finiteness is irrelevant, since the theorem concerns only pure strategies.
Finiteness is sufficient for existence but not necessary.

questions.question: The Nash existence theorem applies to finite normal-form games $\langle N,\{S_i\},\{v_i\}\rangle$. What does 'finite' require?
options: Finitely many players, each with finitely many pure strategies
Finitely many players; strategy sets may be bounded intervals
Payoffs that take only finitely many different values
A game tree that ends after finitely many moves

questions.question: A finite two-player game is checked cell by cell and has no pure-strategy Nash equilibrium. What follows from the Nash existence theorem?
options: It has no Nash equilibrium, since every candidate must first be a pure equilibrium.
It has an equilibrium in which both players use pure strategies after all.
It has an equilibrium in which at least one player gives positive probability to two strategies.
It has infinitely many equilibria, one for each possible mixed strategy of player 1.

questions.question: A one-player game has strategy set $[0,1)$ and payoff $v(s)=s$. It has no Nash equilibrium. Which hypothesis of the Nash existence theorem fails?
options: The number of players is not finite.
The strategy set is not finite.
The payoff function is not linear.
The game has no mixed strategies.

questions.question: In a coordination game payoffs are $(2,2)$ at $(A,A)$, $(1,1)$ at $(B,B)$ and $(0,0)$ otherwise. Both players play $A$ with probability $\tfrac{1}{3}$. What do $A$ and $B$ earn against this, and how many equilibria does the game have?
options: $A$ earns $\tfrac{2}{3}$ and $B$ earns $\tfrac{1}{3}$, so only $(A,A)$ and $(B,B)$ are equilibria
Both earn $\tfrac{2}{3}$, so this is the unique equilibrium that the theorem guarantees
Both earn $\tfrac{2}{3}$, so this is an equilibrium; with $(A,A)$ and $(B,B)$ there are three
Both earn $\tfrac{2}{3}$, so this is an equilibrium; with $(A,A)$, $(B,B)$, $(A,B)$ there are four

questions.question: A one-player game has strategy set $[0,1]$ and payoff $v(s)=s$. Does it have a Nash equilibrium, and does the Nash existence theorem apply?
options: Yes, $s=1$; and the theorem applies, as $[0,1]$ is bounded.
No; the theorem does not apply, so no equilibrium exists.
No; just as on $[0,1)$, every $s$ can be improved.
Yes, $s=1$; but the theorem does not apply, as $[0,1]$ is infinite.

questions.question: A game has three players with $2$, $3$ and $2$ pure strategies. Which object does the Nash existence theorem guarantee?
options: A mixed profile in $\Delta S_1\times\Delta S_2\times\Delta S_3$ of mutual best replies
A profile $s^*\in S_1\times S_2\times S_3$ with each $s_i^*$ a best reply to $s_{-i}^*$
A mixed strategy $\sigma_i^*\in\Delta S_i$ for one player that is best against everything
A probability distribution on $S_1\times S_2\times S_3$ that every player prefers

questions.question: In a finite game, a player's set of mixed strategies $\Delta S_i$ has infinitely many elements whenever $|S_i|\ge2$. Does this conflict with the finiteness hypothesis of the Nash existence theorem?
options: Yes, so the theorem holds only when players use pure strategies
No: the hypothesis concerns the pure-strategy sets $S_i$ only
Yes, unless each player mixes over only two pure strategies
No: $\Delta S_i$ is finite, since probabilities lie in $[0,1]$

questions.question: Why does the Nash existence theorem need mixed strategies rather than only pure strategies?
options: Finite games, such as Matching Pennies, can lack pure equilibria.
Mixed strategies give players higher payoffs than pure ones, which existence requires.
Mixed strategies are needed only to make the number of equilibria finite.
With pure strategies the best-response correspondence is always empty.

questions.question: An analyst shows that some normal-form game has no Nash equilibrium, not even in mixed strategies. What can be concluded?
options: Either the set of players or some player's strategy set must be infinite.
The analyst must have erred, since every game has a Nash equilibrium.
The game has no pure equilibrium, but this is all that can be concluded.
Some player's payoff function is not linear in the pure strategies.

questions.question: In a Cournot duopoly the best-response functions are $BR_1(q_2)=\tfrac{90-q_2}{2}$ and $BR_2(q_1)=\tfrac{90-q_1}{2}$ (for $q_j\le90$). Which profile $(q_1,q_2)$ consists of mutual best responses?
In the Prisoner's Dilemma, $F$ strictly dominates $M$ for both players and $(F,F)$ is the unique Nash equilibrium. What does the Nash existence theorem's guarantee amount to in this game?
options: The pure profile $(F,F)$, read as degenerate mixtures; nothing more is implied.
An additional equilibrium in which both players mix $M$ and $F$.
Nothing, since the theorem applies only to games without pure equilibria.
An equilibrium that improves on $(F,F)$ for both players, such as $(M,M)$.

questions.question: Two firms set prices for identical goods; with prices in an interval a best reply may fail to exist. Suppose instead each firm must choose a whole-euro price in $\{1,2,\ldots,10\}$. Does the Nash existence theorem apply?
options: No: price competition lacks best replies, so no equilibrium can be guaranteed.
Yes, and it guarantees an equilibrium in pure prices.
Yes: two players with finite price sets, so a mixed equilibrium exists.
No: the theorem needs strategy sets that are intervals of real numbers.

questions.question: By the Nash existence theorem a finite game has an equilibrium $\sigma^*$. Which property must every pure strategy $s_i$ that $\sigma_i^*$ plays with positive probability have, against $\sigma_{-i}^*$?
options: It is a best reply to every strategy of the other players
It earns the same as the other used ones, possibly less than an unused one
It is played with the same probability as the other used ones
It earns the highest expected payoff available against $\sigma_{-i}^*$

questions.question: In Matching Pennies player 1 gets $1$ on a match and $-1$ otherwise, and player 2 gets the negative. The theorem guarantees an equilibrium. Can that equilibrium have one player using a pure strategy?
options: Yes: the theorem guarantees that at least one player can use a pure strategy.
No: any pure strategy has a unique best reply, which then prompts a switch.
Yes: player 1 can play $H$ while player 2 mixes half-half.
No: the theorem requires every equilibrium to be fully mixed.

questions.question: Two players each name a positive integer; whoever names the larger number gets $1$ from the other, and a tie pays $0$. Why does the Nash existence theorem not imply that this game has an equilibrium?
options: It does imply one: both naming the same number is an equilibrium with payoff $0$.
Each player has infinitely many strategies, so the theorem does not apply.
It does imply one, since the game has finitely many players and is zero-sum.
The payoffs are not bounded, so the theorem's continuity requirement fails.

questions.question: In Matching Pennies player 1 gets $1$ on a match and $-1$ otherwise, and player 2 gets the negative. With $p=\sigma_1(H)$ and $q=\sigma_2(H)$, $BR_1(q)$ is $p=1$ for $q>\tfrac{1}{2}$, $p=0$ for $q<\tfrac{1}{2}$, all $p$ at $q=\tfrac{1}{2}$; $BR_2(p)$ is $q=0$ for $p>\tfrac{1}{2}$, $q=1$ for $p<\tfrac{1}{2}$, all $q$ at $p=\tfrac{1}{2}$. Where do $BR_1$ and $BR_2$ intersect?
options: Every $(p,q)$ with $p=q$
Only $(\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2})$
None, since both correspondences jump at $\tfrac{1}{2}$
